sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: Turn 4 answers Turn 3 directly: the Lean approach often results in a race to the bottom.
sub.limitation: Turns 1-3 are three separate opening statements, and Turn 8 only gestures back with True, but.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: Turn 5 reframes polish as the current standard of the technological base.
sub.limitation: Turns 7-9 restate the opening positions and add no new distinctions.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: Craft versus validation is surfaced in Turns 4 and 6.
sub.limitation: Never tested for consumer AI specifically, e.g. retention, distribution, or commoditised models.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: Turn 9 tries to combine all three lenses.
sub.limitation: Turn 9 splices the views together without any of them reshaping the others.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: Section D sharpens the question of whether quality is intrinsic or market-adaptive.
sub.limitation: That question is never argued in the turns. It appears only in the summary.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: Turn 8 grants the artist point before qualifying it.
sub.limitation: Turn 4 strawmans Lean as sacrificing quality, though Ries's MVP is about learning, not shoddiness.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: Turn 6 challenges the assumption that technology defines the market.
sub.limitation: Turn 6 asserts its challenge with no evidence or mechanism, and Turn 7 dismisses it without engaging.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: Arthur's combinatorial evolution (Turn 2, Ch. 2) is represented faithfully.
sub.limitation: Turn 7 cites H&P Ch. 10, which covers programming languages, not founders as artists. Turn 3 has Ries say don't build.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: Turn 5 frames quality as a moving target, a hedged interpretive claim.
sub.limitation: Turn 7 says building for yourself is the only way, which is overclaimed. Scare quotes appear in pd=false turns.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: Turn 8 concedes True before adding its caveat.
sub.limitation: Nobody revises a claim, and Turn 9 declares a middle ground without answering Turn 6.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: Section A notes the user is bridging internet-era principles with AI.
sub.limitation: Misses that the user wants to study and learn, not choose a build method.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: Turn 1 references AI trends and API wrappers.
sub.limitation: Consumer (versus B2B) SaaS is never addressed in any turn.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: Section E ties approaches to market conditions.
sub.limitation: The user's goal of drawing principles from the internet age gets no concrete case anywhere.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: Turn 3 mentions running out of runway.
sub.limitation: Generic, since the user's resources, stage and timeline are never considered.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: Section E branches on whether the market is nascent or competitive.
sub.limitation: No focused questions about whether the user has an idea, a team, or is purely researching.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: Turn 7 hints at building what you want for yourself.
sub.limitation: Never asks what the user wants from studying this: to found, to invest, or to understand.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: Turn 6 exposes the tech-first assumption: the market defines the technology.
sub.limitation: The assumption that AI changes consumer SaaS fundamentals is never examined.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: Section D names quality as an intrinsic value versus a market-adaptive variable.
sub.limitation: The turns don't help the user weigh which of these they personally hold.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: Turn 3 alludes to AI hype saturation.
sub.limitation: Pressure to chase AI trends is noted in Turn 1 but never explored.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: Section E offers conditions the user can apply themselves.
sub.limitation: Turn 9's tidy synthesis closes reflection instead of handing the user a question.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: Section E lists the lean, systems and hybrid approaches.
sub.limitation: Options don't fit a study goal: there is no reading path, case set, or learning step.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: Turn 6 says polish is waste if the market doesn't value it.
sub.limitation: The costs of Lean-only and Systems-only approaches are left unstated.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: Section E: a nascent market with transformative AI favours the Systems approach.
sub.limitation: The conditions are broad, and 'well-defined market' is never operationalised.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: Section E has an 'if you remain unsure of your market' branch.
sub.limitation: Consequential unknowns such as model commoditisation and distribution are never separated out.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: Section E: small, high-fidelity experiments.
sub.limitation: A product is presumed and the user's study intent is ignored, with no concrete first step.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: Turn 1 is plain: not just wrapping an API in a nice UI.
sub.limitation: Turns 5 and 8 drift into abstraction, e.g. higher-level assembly of digital components.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: Turn 4 clearly targets the Lean approach.
sub.limitation: Turn 3 says 'You are both', yet neither prior view is engaged specifically.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: All nine turns fall within roughly 40-47 words.
sub.limitation: The uniform length and rigid rotation flatten the rhythm.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: The three stances are clearly separable from the openings on.
sub.limitation: No speaker changes position explicitly. The role name is misspelled as 'Iterater'.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: No extended recaps inside the turns.
sub.limitation: Turns 7 and 8 restate Turns 1 and 2. Single-quote marks break the form rule throughout.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: Turn 4 warns users will abandon it when a better competitor arrives.
sub.limitation: The stakes stay abstract, with no concrete product or user at risk.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: Turn 6 inverts the frame: the market defines the technology.
sub.limitation: There is no real reversal, and the Turn 9 compromise is predictable.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: The Product Obsessive's 'essentially artists' line in Turn 7 has some flair.
sub.limitation: The voices sound like textbook summaries more than distinct temperaments.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: Turn 6: Validate the leap before you build the bridge.
sub.limitation: No vivid examples: no named internet-era product appears anywhere.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: Tension rises slightly across Turns 4-7.
sub.limitation: It deflates at Turn 9 into a consensus without any climax.

strengths: The three lenses (craft, combinatorial evolution, validated learning) are distinct and relevant.
Turn 6 delivers a real counter-assumption, and Section D names the genuine open question about quality.
Turns are concise, evenly paced and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Turn 9 (Lean Iterater) forces a middle ground without resolving Turn 6's challenge.
Grounding is loose: Turn 7 cites H&P Ch. 10 (languages), Turn 3 makes Ries anti-building, and scare quotes appear in pd=false turns.
Ignores the user's study intent and consumer focus, and no internet-era product is examined as a case.
editorNotes: Require at least two named internet-era consumer products as worked examples, analysed for principles that transfer to AI.
Forbid closing compromises unless an earlier objection was explicitly answered or conceded, and require one explicit position revision.
Make the minds address the user's actual goal (study versus build) and ask one focused question about their stage.
Enforce no quotation marks in pd=false turns, and check that the cited chapter actually supports the claim.
